question: True or false: leaving a wider gap after a full stop than between words began with the typewriter?
answer: False. Hand-set printing, above all in the 19th century, often put a wider space after a full stop than between words. Typing manuals copied that habit with the only unit a typewriter had, one fixed character width, so the wide gap became two keystrokes. The typewriter did not invent the gap; it made it countable.
move: Before accepting a tidy origin story, look at what came before it.
ask: Which tidy origin story do I accept without looking at what came before it?
trap: Crediting fixed-width letters, a neat reason that nobody checks against print.
source: Bringhurst, The Elements of Typographic Style
reference: Bringhurst, The Elements of Typographic Style, 3rd edition, Hartley & Marks, 2004
